# Introduction

Most advice about productivity assumes that the problem is a shortage of time. This book begins from a different assumption: the problem is a shortage of attention, and time is merely where we notice it.[^1]

Over the past decade I have worked with more than two hundred teams, and the pattern is remarkably consistent. People do not need more hours. They need one protected hour, used well, every working day.

# Chapter 1: Why Attention Leaks

Attention does not vanish all at once. It leaks, a little at a time, through small openings that each seem harmless.

## The three leaks

In my experience there are three common leaks:

- Notifications that interrupt a task before it has taken shape.
- Meetings scheduled in the middle of the only uninterrupted stretch of the day.
- The habit of checking a message *just in case* it is urgent.

None of these feels expensive in the moment. Together they can consume the whole of a morning.

## A simple test

Try the following for one week:

1. Write down the time whenever you switch tasks.
2. Note what caused the switch.
3. Count the switches at the end of each day.

Most people are surprised by the number. One engineer I worked with counted **sixty-three** switches before lunch.[^2]

# Chapter 2: Building the Quiet Hour

The quiet hour is not complicated. It is a single block of sixty minutes, at the same time each day, in which you work on one thing and nothing else.

## Choosing the hour

Choose the hour when your energy is highest, not the hour that happens to be free. For most people this is early in the day, before the first meeting.

> Protect the hour as you would protect a meeting with your most important client, because that is exactly what it is.

## Keeping it

The first week is the hardest. Colleagues will test the boundary without meaning to, and you will be tempted to make an exception. Do not make the exception. A quiet hour that is negotiable is not a quiet hour at all.

[^1]: This distinction was first drawn clearly in studies of knowledge workers in the late twentieth century.
[^2]: He agreed to let me share the figure on the condition that I did not share his name.
